newsitem.title: USA: Motorola profits hurt by charge for dropping DRAMs.
newsitem.headline: Motorola profits hurt by charge for dropping DRAMs.

text.p: Motorola Inc. on Tuesday said sales grew 10 percent for the second quarter, but the technology giant's profits were hurt, as expected, by a $170 million charge for phasing out its struggling memory chip business.
The company also said it is continuing to review its operations and focus on businesses with the most potential, which could result in further restructuring charges in the second half of the year.

"Motorola continues to build for the future by redirecting resources to development programs with the greatest potential, while focusing on core technology platforms," said Motorola Chief Executive Officer Christopher Galvin.

"We have already taken actions as a result of that process, despite the negative impact of such charges on quarterly financial results. ... We will continue to position the company for sustainable long-term growth and profitability."

Motorola, based in Schaumburg, Ill., said it earned $268 million, or 44 cents per share, in the second quarter ended June 28, below $326 million, or 54 cents per share, a year earlier. Revenues rose to $7.5 billion from $6.8 billion.

Motorola said last week it would take the charge of $170 million, or 18 cents per share, as it exits the business of supplying dynamic random access memory, or DRAM, chips, which have become a low-priced commodity as competitors have mushroomed.
Motorola said it plans to reallocate resources to other technologies.
Net margin on sales fell to 3.6 percent in the second quarter from 4.8 percent a year ago, it said. The first-half net margin slid to 4.2 percent from 5.1 percent.
Excluding the second-quarter charge, Motorola said its operating income rose from the 1996 second quarter, with each business segment reporting increased sales and orders.

Its semiconductor products sales edged up 3 percent to $2.0 billion, while orders rose 36 percent. But the segment reported an operating loss vs. a profit a year ago, because of the $170 million charge.
Motorola's cellular products segment saw sales rise 6 percent to $2.8 billion while orders rose 20 percent.
Sales jumped 22 percent to $1.2 billion for land mobile products sales, and increased 6 percent to $1.1 billion for messaging, information and media products, it said.
Motorola's stock rose $2.125 to $82.50 on the New York Stock Exchange.
